stories.head: Squamish starts work on its first urban forest strategy
stories.dek: The District of Squamish is developing its first Urban Forest Management Strategy. It will guide tree protection, planting and care on public and private land over the next 25 years. A community survey, an online mapping tool and an open house are planned, with details coming soon.
stories.take: Residents will be able to share their views through a survey, nominate valued or heritage trees on a map, and attend an open house once the District posts the details.
stories.body:
## What is happening

The District of Squamish is writing its first Urban Forest Management Strategy. The plan will guide how trees are protected, planted and cared for over the next 25 years. It covers both public and private land.

The urban forest includes trees in yards, along streets, in parks and school grounds, beside rivers and in natural areas. It also includes the soil and other plants that support those trees.

## Why the District says it is needed

As Squamish grows, protecting existing trees and making room for new ones takes coordination. That work spans streets, parks, natural areas and private properties. The District says tree management also has to deal with:

- climate change and wildfire risk
- wildlife habitat
- protecting waterways
- slope stability
- community needs

The strategy will help the District set priorities and plan the resources needed for long term tree care. It will also look at where more trees could give more people shade and access to nature.

## How to take part

The District lists three ways to get involved. Details for each are still to come.

- **Community survey** (coming soon): share what matters to you about local trees, the problems you see, and where efforts should focus.
- **Mapping tool** (coming soon): mark places and trees you value, suggest spots for planting or improvements, and nominate heritage or significant trees. Heritage trees are recognized under the District's Heritage Management Strategy.
- **Community open house** (more information soon): learn about the strategy, ask questions and share ideas.

Updates will be posted on the [Let's Talk Squamish urban forest page](https://letstalksquamish.ca/urban-forest).

## What comes next

Community input will be weighed together with feedback from the Squamish Nation, District Council and staff, and interested groups. The input will shape the strategy's vision, goals and actions. For related coverage, see our [climate and environment](/issues/climate-and-environment/) and [growth and development](/issues/growth-and-development/) pages.

stories.head: Squamish's new council is sworn in Tuesday: what happens, who gets which job, and what comes next
stories.dek: Mayor Sean Easton and six councillors take their oaths on Tuesday, November 3 at 6 p.m. at the Squamish Valley Golf Club, not Municipal Hall. Six of the seven are new to council. On the same night they hand out the first jobs: who fills in as mayor each month, who speaks for Squamish on the regional board, and who sits on the library, community forest and Land Back boards.
stories.take: Anyone can go, but seating is limited, so the District suggests watching the livestream. The ceremony starts at 6:30 p.m. Two weeks later, on November 17, the new council casts its first real votes, and the 2027 budget, now drafted at a 10.4% tax increase, is one of the first big decisions.

visual.small: 6 p.m. meeting, 6:30 ceremony, Squamish Valley Golf Club

src: November 3, 2026 inaugural meeting agenda (District of Squamish)

photo.alt: Mayor Sean Easton and Councillors Eric Andersen, Janice DesJardins, Sarah Ellis, Luc Perreault, Laura Prosko and Shaun Veltkamp
photo.caption: Squamish council for 2026 to 2030.
photo.credit: Campaign photos and District of Squamish; background Straitgate, CC BY-SA 3.0

stories.body:
## Where and when
Tuesday, November 3 at the **Squamish Valley Golf Club, 2458 Mamquam Road**. The meeting opens at 6 p.m. and **the swearing in ceremony starts at 6:30 p.m.** This one meeting is not in Council Chambers.

- **Go in person:** it is open to everyone, but seating is limited. Overflow seating will be in the lobby, and the District is asking people to watch the livestream if they can.
- **Watch live:** [District of Squamish livestream on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/@DistrictofSquamish/streams). The video stays there afterward.
- **Follow by phone or WebEx:** 604 449 3026, access code 2773 519 7595.
- **Agenda:** [inaugural meeting agenda](https://squamish.civicweb.net/document/271675/) and our [meeting page](/meetings/2026-11-03-inaugural/).

A community welcome and reception follow the meeting.

## How the night goes
- A procession of the new council, led by bagpiper Devin Biln and members of the RCMP.
- A Squamish Nation blessing from Allan Harry.
- Judge Sutherland swears in Mayor Easton, then each councillor. Every member also signs on to council's code of conduct.
- Council adopts the agenda and makes its first appointments (below).
- Mayor Easton gives his inaugural address, and each councillor speaks.
- The mayor and each councillor can invite one community member to speak to council for up to three minutes.

## The first jobs council hands out
The agenda leaves every name blank, so these are decided on the night. We will post who got what.
- **Acting mayor:** a councillor for each month from November 2026 to December 2027, who stands in when the mayor is away.
- **Squamish-Lillooet Regional District board:** Mayor Easton holds 5 votes and two councillors hold 4 votes each, plus three backups. It is the regional government for Squamish and the areas around it.
- **Squamish Library Board:** one councillor.
- **Community Forest Board:** two councillors.
- **Land Back Task Force:** three councillors.
- **2027 meeting schedule:** regular council meetings at 6 p.m. in Council Chambers, Municipal Hall, usually the first and third Tuesday, none in August and one in September.

## Who is being sworn in
Easton beat Jenna Stoner by 175 votes, 3,681 to 3,506, with 45% of voters turning out. [Eric Andersen](/council/eric-andersen/) is the only returning councillor; [Sarah Ellis](/council/sarah-ellis/) topped the council vote with 4,499.
- [Mayor Sean Easton](/council/sean-easton/): co executive director of Zero Ceiling, a non profit working to end youth homelessness. Promised to freeze property taxes for 2027.
- [Eric Andersen](/council/eric-andersen/): grew up in Squamish; background in forestry, wood products and transportation. Focus on jobs and businesses keeping pace with growth.
- [Janice DesJardins](/council/janice-desjardins/): long time volunteer whose family has been here since 1912. Wants zero based budgeting and to strive for zero tax increases.
- [Sarah Ellis](/council/sarah-ellis/): executive director of Housing Squamish. Focus on homes people can afford to rent or own.
- [Luc Perreault](/council/luc-perreault/): civil engineering technologist, public works inspector and former firefighter. Focus on infrastructure and transparency.
- [Laura Prosko](/council/laura-prosko/): runs the Central Lonsdale business association in North Vancouver. Focus on housing, small business and the Woodfibre and FortisBC partnerships.
- [Shaun Veltkamp](/council/shaun-veltkamp/): Squamish business owner for more than 20 years. Focus on housing, green spaces and trades jobs.

## What comes next
- **November 17:** the first regular council meeting, and the first votes. We post how each member voted [the same night](/meetings/2026-11-17-regular/), and you can [vote on the same questions first](/have-your-say/).
- **The 2027 budget:** staff have drafted a 10.4% property tax increase, and this council decides it, with adoption expected early in 2027. That is the first big test of the tax promises above.
- **Promises:** we track [67 promises and every campaign position](/scorecard/) against how each member actually votes.
- New to how council works? Our [plain guide](/how-council-works/) covers the first 100 days.

stories.head: Wind warning for southern Howe Sound with gusts up to 90 km/h this morning
stories.dek: Environment Canada has issued a wind warning for southern sections of Howe Sound, including Bowen Island. Northerly winds of 70 km/h gusting to 90 km/h are expected to develop early this morning. Winds should ease late this morning, but will stay blustery into this evening. Local power outages are possible, and flying or falling debris could cause injury.
stories.take: Secure loose objects outside and be ready to adjust your driving for changing conditions, and you can report severe weather to BCstorm@ec.gc.ca or with #BCStorm on social media.

photo.alt: Howe Sound seen from above Squamish
photo.caption: Howe Sound, seen from above Squamish.

stories.body:
## What is happening

Environment Canada has put out a wind warning for the southern parts of Howe Sound. The warning area includes Bowen Island.

Strong winds from the north are expected to start early this morning. Here is what the forecast says:

- Steady winds of 70 km/h
- Gusts up to 90 km/h
- Winds should ease late this morning
- It will stay blustery into this evening

## Possible effects

Winds this strong can cause problems. Environment Canada says:

- Local power outages are possible
- Flying or falling debris could hurt people

## What you can do

Environment Canada suggests a few simple steps:

- Tie down or bring in loose objects outside, like patio furniture, garbage bins and garden items
- Be ready to change how you drive if conditions change quickly

If you see severe weather, you can report it to Environment Canada. Send an email to BCstorm@ec.gc.ca, or post on social media using #BCStorm.

## Where to check for updates

Weather warnings can change during the day. For the latest local conditions, including weather, Highway 99, river levels and air quality, see our [today page](/today/). You can also check the [Environment Canada forecast for Squamish](https://weather.gc.ca/en/location/index.html?coords=49.702,-123.156).

stories.head: Valeriote leads West Vancouver to Sea to Sky after the first count; Conservatives lead across B.C.
stories.dek: After the initial count, Jeremy Valeriote of the BC Green Party leads the riding by about 2,000 votes. Across British Columbia the Conservative Party leads in enough ridings for a majority. Valeriote is one of two Green candidates leading. Elections BC does the final count November 6 to 10, so these results are not final.
stories.take: If the final count holds, your member of the Legislature will sit in opposition to a Conservative government.

visual.title: West Vancouver to Sea to Sky, votes
visual.note: All 90 ballot boxes counted. Preliminary until Elections BC declares official results.

photo.alt: Sea to Sky Highway curving along Howe Sound at Porteau Road
photo.caption: The Sea to Sky Highway along Howe Sound, part of the West Vancouver to Sea to Sky riding.

stories.body:
## The local result

All 90 ballot boxes in West Vancouver to Sea to Sky have been counted in the initial count. Jeremy Valeriote of the BC Green Party is ahead. These are the preliminary numbers:

- BC Green Party (Jeremy Valeriote): 10,503 votes
- Conservative Party: 8,478 votes
- BC NDP (New Democratic Party): 2,283 votes
- All other candidates: 818 votes

That puts Valeriote 2,025 votes ahead of the Conservative candidate. Valeriote is one of only two Green candidates leading anywhere in B.C.

## Across British Columbia

Elections BC reports that 100 per cent of ballot boxes across the province have reported. The parties are leading in this many ridings:

- Conservative Party: 63 ridings, 862,688 votes (48.06 per cent)
- BC NDP: 28 ridings, 670,811 votes (37.37 per cent)
- BC Green Party: 2 ridings, 196,896 votes (10.97 per cent)

No other party is leading in any riding. CentreBC has 29,104 votes (1.62 per cent) and OneBC has 27,056 votes (1.51 per cent). Independent candidates have 3,202 votes in total.

In all, 1,799,550 votes were considered. There were 3,738,182 registered voters as of October 14, 2026. That makes the preliminary voter turnout 48.14 per cent.

## Why these results are not final

Elections BC says results from the initial count are preliminary. They can still change as they are checked for accuracy and completeness.

Some ballots have not been counted yet:

- Ballots sent by mail
- Absentee ballots

These will be counted at the final count. Elections BC does extra checks on these ballots to make sure only eligible voters vote, and that each person votes only once.

## What comes next

- Final count: November 6 to 10, 2026
- Results become official only when Elections BC declares them

If the final count matches the initial count, the riding's member of the Legislature will be a Green member sitting in opposition to a Conservative government.

You can follow the results on the [Elections BC results page](https://results.elections.bc.ca/).

stories.head: Final count: Easton wins mayor by 175 votes, and six of seven seats change hands
stories.dek: The official count confirms Sean Easton beat Jenna Stoner 3,681 to 3,506. Eric Andersen is the only councillor returning. Sarah Ellis led the council vote with 4,499. Councillors John French, Andrew Hamilton and Chris Pettingill were not elected.
stories.take: Six of the seven members are new to council. What each of them promised is on our scorecard.
stories.body:
## The mayor's race

The District of Squamish released the Chief Election Officer's final results on October 21, 2026. In total, 8,881 ballots were cast. Turnout was 45.33%.

[Sean Easton](/council/sean-easton/) won the mayor's seat. Jenna Stoner, a councillor on the outgoing council, came second. Daniel Deal came third.

- Sean Easton: 3,681 votes (41.93%), elected
- Jenna Stoner: 3,506 votes (39.94%)
- Daniel Deal: 1,591 votes (18.12%)

Here is how each candidate's votes broke down by when people voted:

- Easton: 1,169 at advance voting, 52 by mail or special voting, 2,460 on voting day
- Stoner: 1,237 at advance voting, 53 by mail or special voting, 2,216 on voting day
- Deal: 488 at advance voting, 20 by mail or special voting, 1,083 on voting day

Stoner had more advance votes than Easton. Easton had more votes on voting day.

## The council race

Fifteen people ran for six councillor seats. These six were elected:

- [Sarah Ellis](/council/sarah-ellis/): 4,499
- [Eric Andersen](/council/eric-andersen/): 3,851
- [Laura Prosko](/council/laura-prosko/): 3,828
- [Luc Perreault](/council/luc-perreault/): 3,785
- [Shaun Veltkamp](/council/shaun-veltkamp/): 3,754
- [Janice DesJardins](/council/janice-desjardins/): 3,688

These candidates were not elected:

- A. John Lowe: 3,012
- Anders Ourom: 2,975
- John French: 2,697
- Ian Brown: 2,648
- Andrew Hamilton: 2,607
- Chris Pettingill: 2,460
- Sean Goodwin: 1,802
- Kieran Brownie: 1,632
- Chris Ryan: 1,077

Three sitting councillors ran again and lost: John French, Andrew Hamilton and Chris Pettingill. Eric Andersen is the only councillor coming back. DesJardins, in sixth place, finished 676 votes ahead of A. John Lowe in seventh.

## What comes next

- The new council will be sworn in on November 3, 2026, at 6 p.m. at the Squamish Valley Golf Club, 2458 Mamquam Road. See the [inaugural meeting page](/meetings/2026-11-03-inaugural/).
- The first regular council meeting is on November 17, 2026, in Council Chambers at Municipal Hall, 37955 Second Avenue. See the [November 17 meeting page](/meetings/2026-11-17-regular/).

Each member's page lists what they promised during the campaign. You can track those promises against their votes on our [scorecard](/scorecard/). Our [full results page](/results/) has every number. The official results are on the [District of Squamish election page](https://squamish.ca/government-and-administration/council/election/).

stories.head: Proposed 2027 budget is online before council votes on it
stories.dek: The District posted its proposed 2027 budget and 10 year financial plan, project by project. The same week it received the Government Finance Officers Association's Distinguished Budget Presentation Award for its 2026 budget document.
stories.take: The budget sets property tax and utility rates. Council has not adopted it yet.

visual.small: Length of the District's financial plan

photo.alt: Aerial view of Squamish with mountains behind
photo.caption: Squamish from above.

stories.body:
## What is online

The District of Squamish has posted its draft 2027 to 2036 financial plan in an online tool called Budget Book. You can find it at [letstalksquamish.ca/budget-2027](https://letstalksquamish.ca/budget-2027). The tool shows proposed projects, changes to service levels and budget pressures that council will look at before it adopts the plan. The current plan, for 2026 to 2035, is also there to compare.

On October 20, 2026, the District said it received the Government Finance Officers Association's Distinguished Budget Presentation Award for its 2026 budget document. The District calls this the highest recognition in government budgeting. Read the [District news release](https://squamish.ca/government-and-administration/district-information/news/district-receives-government-finance-officers-association-distinguished-budget-presentation-award/).

## The numbers so far

A council agenda from September 29, 2026 shows where the staff draft stands:

- The draft general fund starts at a 10.4% [property tax](/issues/property-taxes/) increase, before items still waiting for council approval.
- 6.6% of that is costs the District has already committed to.
- That works out to about $342 more for the average home.
- Nothing is decided. The new council sets the final number, likely in January 2027.

In January 2026, council adopted the District's first 10 year financial plan. It raised property tax revenue 12.8% in 2026 ([our explainer](/explained/why-squamish-property-taxes-went-up-12-8-percent/)). The District says the main costs behind the increases are aging buildings that must be replaced (the public works yard, fire halls and [Brennan Park](/issues/brennan-park-and-recreation/)), RCMP contract costs, wages, debt payments and building up savings.

## Why this year is different

Budget talks began in early September with council workshops. Because of the election, the old council reviewed the draft until the end of its term. The new council will pick up the review.

During the campaign, Mayor [Sean Easton](/council/sean-easton/) promised to freeze property taxes for 2027. Councillor [Janice DesJardins](/council/janice-desjardins/) said she wants zero based budgeting and to strive for zero tax increases. You can follow these promises on our [scorecard](/scorecard/).

## How to take part

- Explore the draft plan in [Budget Book](https://letstalksquamish.ca/budget-2027).
- Answer the questions on the Let's Talk Squamish budget page.
- Email comments to budgetfeedback@squamish.ca.
- Watch council budget meetings live or as recordings on CivicWeb.
- Click "+ Follow" on the budget page for updates.
- Attend a Budget Information Night to meet council and staff. The date has not been set yet.

The District says all feedback will go to the new council during budget talks. After input closes, it will publish a What We Heard Report on the main themes. You can also weigh in on our [Have your say](/have-your-say/) page.

stories.head: Community grants open to local nonprofits until November 16
stories.dek: The Squamish Community Foundation is taking applications for 2027 Community Enhancement Grants on behalf of the District. Eligible projects include neighbourhood events, youth programs, reconciliation, recreation and climate action. Arts projects apply to Squamish Arts instead, and a group can receive one grant or the other.
stories.take: Nonprofits and charities are eligible. Individuals and businesses are not.

photo.alt: Shops along Cleveland Avenue in downtown Squamish
photo.caption: Cleveland Avenue, downtown Squamish.

stories.body:
## What the grants are for

The District of Squamish runs a Community Enhancement Grant program. It gives money to nonprofit and charitable groups for projects that improve life for people in Squamish. The Squamish Community Foundation runs the program for council. Applications for 2027 grants are open now, and the deadline is November 16.

The program supports the District's Official Community Plan. The goal is a more liveable, healthy, engaged, connected and resilient community.

Projects can fit into any of these areas:

- Decolonization and reconciliation
- Community and neighbourhood events
- Programs that bring different generations together
- Better connections between neighbourhoods
- Caring for the environment, sustainability or climate action
- Diversity, equity and inclusion programs
- Physical health, mental health or social wellbeing
- Projects led by youth
- Social services for people in Squamish who are vulnerable
- Recreation programs

## Who can apply

Nonprofits and charities can apply. Individuals and businesses cannot.

The District works with two local groups on its grants. Projects about arts or culture should apply to the Arts and Culture Grant from Squamish Arts instead. A group can get money from only one of the two programs. If a project could fit both, the group can email info@squamishartscouncil.com or info@squamishfoundation.com to find out which one to use.

## How to apply

The 2027 application form and applicant guide can be downloaded from the [Squamish Community Foundation website](https://www.squamishfoundation.com/ceg/). Questions can go to info@squamishfoundation.com or 604-848-8683.

Groups that got a grant in 2026 must hand in a report by January 31, 2027. A report template is on the same page.

## Who got money in 2026

In 2026, the program gave out a total of $115,900 to 32 organizations. Many groups got $2,000. Some of the larger amounts were:

- Squamish Helping Hands Society: $10,000
- PearlSpace Support Services Society: $8,000
- BIPOC Rocks: $5,700
- Squamish Climate Action Network: $5,500
- MakeWay Charitable Society, for the Átl'ka7tsem / Howe Sound Marine Stewardship Initiative: $5,000
- Sea to Sky Community Services, for Healthy Pregnancy Outreach: $5,000
- Squamish Search and Rescue: $5,000
- Bike Society of Squamish: $4,500

Other 2026 recipients included sports clubs, the Squamish 55+ Community Society, Sea to Sky Hospice Society, the Squamish Lil'wat Cultural Centre and two projects at Howe Sound Secondary School.

stories.head: Paula de Jong elected Area D director
stories.dek: Area D covers rural land around Squamish, including the Squamish Valley, Upper Squamish, Furry Creek and Britannia Beach. De Jong joins the regional district board November 26.

photo.alt: The Squamish River winding through a forested valley
photo.caption: The Squamish River valley, part of Area D.

stories.body:
## What happened

Paula de Jong has been elected as the director for Electoral Area D of the Squamish-Lillooet Regional District. She won by a vote of Area D residents.

The Chief Election Officer declared the official results for Area D at 4:00 p.m. on Tuesday, October 20, 2026. The official results for Area D are posted as a PDF on the [regional district election results page](https://www.slrd.bc.ca/inside-slrd/legislative-services/general-local-elections/2026-general-local-election-results).

## About Area D

Area D is rural land around Squamish. It is not part of the District of Squamish, so Area D residents do not vote for Squamish council. They elect their own director to the regional district board instead.

Area D includes:

- the Squamish Valley
- Upper Squamish
- Furry Creek
- Britannia Beach

De Jong will join the regional district board on November 26.

## Results in the other areas

The regional district also posted results for its other electoral areas:

- Area A: John Courchesne was elected by a vote.
- Area B: Vivian Birch-Jones was elected by acclamation, which means no vote was needed.
- Area C: Veronica Woodruff was elected by acclamation.

The official results for Area A were declared at the same time as Area D, at 4:00 p.m. on October 20.

## Questions about the election

People with questions or comments about the regional district election can contact its election office:

- Phone: 604-894-6371
- Email: election@slrd.bc.ca
- Mail: Box 219, 1350 Aster Street, Pemberton BC, V0N 2L0

For results in the District of Squamish itself, see our [results page](/results/) and the page for [Mayor Sean Easton](/council/sean-easton/). The new Squamish council holds its [inaugural meeting on November 3](/meetings/2026-11-03-inaugural/).

stories.head: Outgoing council's final meeting reviews its strategic plan
stories.dek: One agenda item: a summary report on the 2023 to 2026 Strategic Plan. Compare it with recorded votes on our scorecard.

photo.alt: Downtown Squamish street with the Stawamus Chief behind
photo.caption: Downtown Squamish, with the Stawamus Chief behind.

stories.body:
## What happens

The outgoing council holds a Special Business Meeting on October 20, 2026. The agenda has one item: a staff report called "2023-2026 Strategic Plan Summary." It is for information only, so council is not asked to vote on it. You can read the full report in the [October 20 council agenda](https://squamish.civicweb.net/Portal/MeetingInformation.aspx?Org=Cal&Id=2115).

The plan had four goals. The report lists what the District says it got done under each one.

## People and relationships

This goal was about building inclusion and belonging. Work listed includes:

- A Memorandum of Understanding between the Squamish Nation (Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw) and the District
- A Land Back Task Force and a formal apology for past harms to the Squamish Nation
- The Squamish Strong Protocol Agreement (Wa Iy̓ím ta Sḵwx̱wú7mesh)
- An Inclusive Hiring and Onboarding Program and ongoing work on the Accessibility Plan
- The Mén̓mens ta smánit childcare facility in Valleycliffe

## Parks, housing and transit

This goal was about a connected and livable community. The report lists:

- The Brennan Park green and accessibility retrofit, six new pickleball courts and three repaired tennis courts (see our [Brennan Park and recreation](/issues/brennan-park-and-recreation/) page)
- Sp’akw’us Feather Park, and Phase 2 of Miyíw̓ts Waterfront Landing Park, with Phase 3 under construction
- The Garibaldi Estates Neighbourhood Plan, new Amenity Cost Charge and Development Cost Charge bylaws, and all actions in the Squamish Housing Action Plan (see [housing](/issues/housing/))
- Phase 1 of the Adventure Centre Revitalization
- Lower speed limits and a Traffic Calming Policy
- More HandyDart and fixed route bus service, a new OnDemand service and progress on a transit maintenance facility (see [transit and Highway 99](/issues/transit-and-highway-99/))
- A paid [parking](/issues/parking/) pilot project

## Services and money

Under reliable service delivery, the District says it:

- Adopted its first 10 Year Financial Plan
- Brought in a Property Tax Policy (see [property taxes](/issues/property-taxes/))
- Rebuilt the Squamish.ca website to be easier to use
- Finished building the new Public Works Facility
- Mostly finished upgrades to the Wastewater Treatment Plant

## Climate and the future

The plan aimed to cut community greenhouse gas emissions by 45% by 2030. The report lists:

- An updated Community Climate Action Plan
- Fire Hall No. 2, built as a net zero building
- A Memorandum of Understanding with Squamish Capilano University
- The Cheekeye Fan Debris Flow Mitigation Review
- Construction progress on the X̱wún̓eḵw Park Sea Dike, and upgrades to the Squamish River Dike at Jimmy Jimmy Slough (see [flood protection](/issues/flood-protection/))

To compare these results with how members actually voted, see our [scorecard](/scorecard/).

stories.head: Turnout rises to 45 percent, with 2,163 more voters than 2022
stories.dek: 8,881 people voted from a list of 19,591 eligible electors. April Lowe and Leanne Roderick were elected school trustees.
stories.take: About 55 percent of eligible voters did not vote. Every race is on our results page.

photo.alt: Main street in Squamish with snowy peaks behind
photo.caption: Downtown Squamish.

stories.body:
## Who was elected

The District of Squamish posted the unofficial results of the 2026 general election on October 17, 2026. Voters chose one mayor, six councillors and two school trustees.

- Mayor: [Sean Easton](/council/sean-easton/)
- Councillors: [Sarah Ellis](/council/sarah-ellis/), [Eric Andersen](/council/eric-andersen/), [Laura Prosko](/council/laura-prosko/), [Luc Perreault](/council/luc-perreault/), [Shaun Veltkamp](/council/shaun-veltkamp/) and [Janice DesJardins](/council/janice-desjardins/)
- School trustees: April Lowe and Leanne Roderick

The results were unofficial until the Chief Election Officer made a final decision later in the week.

## How turnout compares with 2022

The District counted turnout after adding everyone who registered to vote during the election.

- 2026: 8,881 ballots cast from 19,591 registered eligible electors, a turnout of 45.33 percent
- 2022: 6,718 ballots cast from 16,337 registered eligible electors, a turnout of 41.1 percent

That means 2,163 more ballots were cast than in 2022. The list of eligible electors also grew between the two elections.

## How people voted for mayor

The official results were declared on October 21, 2026. They show how many votes each mayor candidate got at advance voting, by special or mail ballot, and on voting day.

- Sean Easton: 1,169 advance, 52 special or mail, 2,460 on voting day (3,681 in all)
- Jenna Stoner: 1,237 advance, 53 special or mail, 2,216 on voting day (3,506 in all)
- Daniel Deal: 488 advance, 20 special or mail, 1,083 on voting day (1,591 in all)

Jenna Stoner got more advance votes than Sean Easton. Sean Easton got more votes on voting day.

You can see every race on our [results page](/results/). The full release is on the [District of Squamish website](https://squamish.ca/government-and-administration/district-information/news/squamish-2026-general-election-unofficial-results/).

## What comes next

The new council will be sworn in at the [inaugural council meeting](/meetings/2026-11-03-inaugural/).

- Date: November 3, 2026
- Time: 6 p.m.
- Place: Squamish Valley Golf Club, 2458 Mamquam Road

To learn how council meetings and votes work, read our [plain guide to council](/how-council-works/). Our [scorecard](/scorecard/) will check campaign promises against how council members vote.

stories.head: District permanently closes Third and Main encampment site
stories.dek: The District reversed its plan to let residents return after a September 18 fire and propane tank ignitions near Under One Roof, which houses supportive housing, an emergency shelter and the food bank. Fire Chief Aaron Foote also cited limited access for emergency crews.
stories.take: Under One Roof has 40 residents, 20 shelter users and 70 staff, according to the District.

visual.alt: Map of downtown Squamish marking Third Avenue and Main Street
visual.cap: The site at Third Avenue and Main Street.

stories.body:
## What happened

The District of Squamish has reversed an earlier decision about the encampment site at Third Avenue and Main Street. People who were living at the site will not be allowed to go back. The District says it is closing the site permanently to any future encampment. Encampment residents are being told about the change.

The change follows a fire and propane tank ignitions behind Under One Roof on September 18. The District says the fire raised serious fire safety concerns for the building, the services it offers and the people inside it.

## Why the District made the change

Under One Roof is Squamish's only supportive housing, shelter and food bank facility. According to the District, the building has:

- 40 residents
- 20 emergency shelter users
- 70 staff

"The recent fire and explosions heightened existing concerns about the proximity of the encampment site to Squamish's only supportive housing, shelter and food bank facility," said Squamish Fire Rescue Chief Aaron Foote. He added that getting in and out of the site "was extremely challenging" for fire crews, RCMP and emergency services, because residents needed help to leave the site.

## Support for people who were displaced

The District says it is still working with outreach workers to help people who had to leave the encampment. Help being offered includes:

- short-term places to stay at Under One Roof
- other alternate accommodations
- tents and tarps

Lori Pyne, Executive Director of Squamish Helping Hands, said the people affected are "some of our community's most vulnerable" and that the move may be unsettling for them. "Closing this site doesn't solve the underlying challenges they face, it simply changes where they are," she said. She said her group will keep working with the District and its partners to connect people with the resources they need.

## A new site at Vancouver Street and Loggers Lane

The District says it knows some encampment residents have moved to a site at the corner of Vancouver Street and Loggers Lane. The District owns land in that area. It plans to put in:

- a portable toilet
- a bear-proof waste bin

## More information

The District has answers to common questions about this work, and about supportive and transitional housing projects in Squamish, at [squamish.ca/addressing-homelessness](https://squamish.ca/addressing-homelessness). You can read the full [District of Squamish news release](https://squamish.ca/government-and-administration/district-information/news/fire-safety-concerns-have-resulted-in-a-reversal-of-the-decision-on-the-future-of-the-encampment/).

For more coverage, see our pages on [homelessness](/issues/homelessness/) and [housing](/issues/housing/).

stories.head: District of Squamish formally apologizes to the Squamish Nation
stories.dek: The District apologized to the Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw for harms caused by District actions over generations, including loss of language, culture and economic opportunity. It was given privately at Totem Hall on September 19 and marked publicly at O'Siyam Pavilion on the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation.
stories.take: The apology came from the True Words project (ta wanáxw sníchim) and is one of six shared priorities in the District and Nation's agreement.

photo.alt: The Stawamus Chief seen from the Chief Overlook trail
photo.caption: The Stawamus Chief (Siyám Smánit), seen from the Chief Overlook trail.

stories.body:
## What happened

The District of Squamish has formally acknowledged the harms done to generations of the Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw (Squamish Nation) by colonial systems and policies. The District also apologized for its own actions that denied the Squamish People their wellbeing, culture, economy, governance and full enjoyment of Squamish rights and title.

The apology was shared at two ceremonies:

- **September 19:** a private ceremony at Totem Hall, where the acknowledgement and apology were delivered
- **September 30:** a public ceremony at O'Siyam Pavilion on the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation

## What the apology says

Part of the apology reads: "The District of Squamish recognizes the racism and discrimination experienced by generations of Sḵwx̱wú7mesh People, the loss of Sḵwx̱wú7mesh language and culture, and the lack of respect shown for the sacredness of the lands and waters. We know that colonization negatively impacted the economic development of the Sḵwx̱wú7mesh People."

It goes on: "To all Sḵwx̱wú7mesh People: we are sorry. We are sorry for the harms that you, your families, your communities and your ancestors have experienced, and you continue to experience."

## How it came about

The apology was shaped by the ta wanáxw sníchim (True Words) Project. The project had two parts:

- The District looked through its own archival records.
- The Squamish Nation led oral history interviews.

The goal was to understand the past and ongoing harms the District may have caused Squamish Nation People. The research and its results are set out in the ta wanáxw sníchim Report.

The apology is one of six priority activities in the Memorandum of Understanding the District and the Nation signed on July 22, 2025. The agreement builds on decades of working together. It covers shared work on land stewardship, reconciliation and joint decision making.

## What leaders said

Sxwíxwtn Wilson Williams, Chairperson of the Squamish Nation, said the apology "represents a significant step forward" in the work the two governments have done since signing the agreement. "Throughout this process, the District of Squamish has opened its heart and mind to our People, and that openness has grounded this work in genuine respect and understanding," he said.

Mayor Armand Hurford said: "Reconciliation is grounded in truth and the Formal Apology is a significant step forward in our continued path with the Squamish Nation." He thanked the Nation's elders and knowledge keepers "who shared their stories, teachings and truth as part of this important work."

## Read it and what comes next

The full acknowledgement and apology, and the ta wanáxw sníchim Report, are online at [squamish.ca/formal-apology](https://squamish.ca/formal-apology). You can also read the [District's news release](https://squamish.ca/government-and-administration/district-information/news/district-of-squamish-delivers-formal-apology-to-squamish-nation-for-inter-generational-harms/).

At its [inaugural meeting on November 3, 2026](/meetings/2026-11-03-inaugural/), the new council will appoint three councillors to the Land Back Task Force.

stories.head: Province and Sea to Sky communities sign agreement to plan a corridor bus
stories.dek: The Sea to Sky Regional Transit Committee and the Province agreed to work on how a bus from Líl̓wat Nation to Metro Vancouver would be governed, funded and run.
stories.take: This is a planning agreement. It does not yet fund or schedule any buses.

visual.alt: Map of the proposed bus route from Lil'wat Nation through Pemberton, Whistler and Squamish to Vancouver
visual.cap: Proposed route, drawn as straight lines between stops.

stories.body:
## What was signed

The Sea to Sky Regional Transit Committee signed a memorandum of understanding with the Province of British Columbia. The District of Squamish announced it on September 22, 2026.

The agreement says the two sides will work together on planning an interregional transit service. That service would link Sea to Sky corridor communities, running from Líl̓wat Nation to Metro Vancouver along Highway 99 (the Sea to Sky Highway).

The agreement supports work on three things for the service:

- How it would be governed
- How it would be funded
- How the service would be set up and run

## Who is on the committee

Six partners work together on the Sea to Sky Regional Transit Committee:

- Líl̓wat Nation
- Village of Pemberton
- Squamish-Lillooet Regional District
- Resort Municipality of Whistler
- District of Squamish
- Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw (Squamish Nation)

The committee was formed in 2019. Its goal is a regional transit service along the corridor between Líl̓wat Nation and Metro Vancouver. The partners have worked with the Province for more than a decade on this.

## How the idea started

- **2015:** The Sea to Sky Transit Future Plan first pointed to an interregional service. BC Transit made the plan with the public and regional partners, based on a lot of community input.
- **2017:** That plan led to the Regional Transit Study. It looked at options for an interregional bus in the short and medium term.
- **2019:** The study led to the creation of the committee.

## What the agreement says

The agreement notes a shared interest in a service on Highway 99 that would:

- Better connect communities
- Meet demand from commuters
- Reduce traffic congestion
- Give fair access to goods and services

It also lists guiding principles from the Province. These include decisions made at the regional level, linking different kinds of passenger transportation, using funding from partners, cooperation between private companies and government, and fair access for everyone.

Jen Ford, Board Chair of the Squamish-Lillooet Regional District, spoke for the committee. "Reliable and accessible regional transit is essential for connecting people with employment, education, healthcare, recreation, and services throughout our region," she said.

## What it does not do yet

This is a planning agreement only. The news release does not announce any funding, bus routes or start date for a service.

Read the full [District of Squamish news release](https://squamish.ca/government-and-administration/district-information/news/memorandum-of-understanding-to-continue-advancing-interregional-transit-signed/). For more on this topic, see our [transit and Highway 99](/issues/transit-and-highway-99/) page.
